content:
Jony Ive and Sam Altman have been keeping everyone on tenterhooks about their AI hardware device, but it looks like the teasing started way too early. People still don't expect to see an official product launch, with the earliest possibility being next year.

OpenAI continues to maintain an extremely vague stance on the form of its first hardware device, but an interview yesterday seemed to reveal that the product is quite similar to a HomePad...

Apple's upcoming "HomePad"

We've always expected Apple to launch a brand-new smart home device that combines a smart speaker with a screen. Since it sounds like a hybrid of HomePod and iPad, we've been calling it HomePad (though some reports suggest it might launch under the HomePod Touch brand).

The device may offer both wall-mounting and placement on a kitchen counter or desk, and it looks likely to launch alongside the new iPhone this September.

OpenAI's mysterious hardware device

Ive and Altman made a lot of big claims in a disappointing teaser video over a year ago for OpenAI's upcoming hardware device. In particular, they strongly hinted that the product would be an entirely new product form factor never seen before, unlike any smart device we've encountered.

However, independent reports suggest these claims might be overhyped even by tech industry standards. Recent reports indicate the product may simply be a smart speaker with a built-in camera, capable of doing things similar to Visual Intelligence or Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

Latest clues

The company is sticking to its strategy of keeping the product mysterious, but when journalist Joanna Stern interviewed OpenAI president Greg Brockman yesterday, at least one potential clue emerged.

Brockman deflected the question to ChatGPT, but he neither denied ChatGPT's response nor denied Stern's mention of a smart speaker.

ChatGPT: The way I see it, it's something ambient, low-friction, voice-first but not just voice, with clear privacy signals. Stern: What do you think about reports calling it a smart speaker? Brockman: Well, I can tell you we're building a family of devices, right?

When Stern asked whether the device needs a screen, Brockman replied: "You'll find out then." Whether this was a hint of wordplay or just casual phrasing is unclear, but I find it interesting that he didn't outright deny it. Put it this way—if people think your product will have a screen but you have no plans to include one, you'd want to clarify that early so no one sets their expectations too high.
